messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Workplace: Workplace, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Raymond Okafor was a 55-year-old African American man who came to treatment several months after his wife died suddenly, leaving him with a PCL-5 score of 67 and a life that, in his words, no longer felt like his own. The death had been unexpected and traumatic: one evening she had collapsed at home, and by the time the ambulance arrived there was nothing anyone could do. Raymond could still picture the blur of that night in pieces — the hallway light, the stretcher, the flashing emergency lights outside the house — but just as often he was hit by the raw feeling of it without a clear picture at all, a surge of panic and grief that seemed to rise out of nowhere. From the start, ambulance sirens, talk of other people losing loved ones, and even the sight of the workplace where he painted houses were enough to pull him back toward that night. A passing ambulance on the street could make his chest tighten and his thoughts race to his wife; a conversation at work about someone’s mother or brother dying could leave him staring blankly at a wall, overwhelmed by the same grief he felt when he first heard she was gone. He noticed that remembering the event was rarely a calm recollection. The memories came as vivid images — his wife on the floor, the paramedics kneeling beside her, the look on the faces of neighbors gathered outside — and once those images surfaced, he felt emotionally flooded and then immediately on guard, as if danger were still unfolding in front of him.

Over time Raymond came to believe that the trauma had not simply taken his wife but had taken something essential from him as well. He said he did not know himself anymore and felt set apart from other people, especially when coworkers joked about family or spoke casually about the future. That sense that his life had been destroyed sat heavily with him and made ordinary moments feel contaminated by loss. It also sharpened his vigilance. At night, when the house was quiet and his wife’s absence was most obvious, he found it harder to feel safe than during the day; he lay awake listening for sounds from outside, body tense and ready to react, and even inside his own home he felt on guard. He noticed that the more he told himself he was broken and isolated, the more his body stayed braced for danger, as if his mind were warning him that something terrible could happen again at any moment. Those beliefs fed back into the memories too. When he tried to think about his wife, the pictures came quickly, but they were often followed by a blank, unbearable emotional wave that confirmed for him that the loss had shattered him. In those moments he would be flooded with the conviction that his life had been ruined beyond repair.

Raymond also began to manage his distress by avoiding the places and topics that set it off, though the relief never lasted. He started taking different routes to avoid ambulances whenever possible and found himself pulling away from conversations at work that turned to illness, funerals, or other people’s bereavements. At his painting job, which should have kept him busy, he became uneasy around the rhythm of the workplace itself — the noise of engines, the sight of service vehicles pulling up near a site, even the mention of a colleague being late because of an emergency. Each of these moments could spark the same chain: the trigger would bring back the images or the emotional force of his wife’s death, the memories would make him feel exposed and unsafe, and the feeling of being changed and alone would push him to keep his distance from people and places that might remind him of what happened. He gradually spent less time chatting with coworkers and more time working in silence, which only deepened the sense that he was apart from others.

By the time he sought help, Raymond was sleeping poorly, checking the doors at night, and feeling constantly keyed up in a way that made him exhausted and irritable. He described moving through his days with the sense that the world could break open without warning, and that anything connected to ambulances, his work, or stories of loss could drag him back into the most painful parts of that night. What brought him in was the fear that he was becoming unreachable even to himself, and what he most hoped for was some way to feel safe in his own home again without being ambushed by the pictures, the grief, and the certainty that his life had ended when his wife died.
